title: Indian Markets Post Best Day in Two Months. Oil Crashed. The Rupee Rallied. Foreign Money May Follow.
excerpt: Sensex surged 1,695 points and the rupee hit 95.11 as Brent crude fell below $87 on hopes of a US-Iran peace deal. Analysts say the record $30 billion in foreign outflows may finally reverse.
body:
The Sensex surged 1,695 points on Friday — its largest single-day gain in two months — closing at 75,528 as Brent crude plunged below $87 a barrel on growing expectations that the United States and Iran are about to sign a peace deal. All 30 Sensex stocks ended in the green. The Nifty 50 rose 461 points, or 1.99 per cent, to 23,623.

The rally added more than ₹7 lakh crore to the market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies, pushing the total close to ₹460 lakh crore. For a market that has shed 6.2 per cent since the Iran war erupted in late February, it was the clearest sign yet that the geopolitical risk premium is beginning to unwind.

## The Oil Price Collapse Driving Sentiment

Brent crude fell roughly 4 per cent during the session, settling at $87.33 a barrel — its lowest level since early March. WTI dropped 3.2 per cent to $84.88, the weakest since mid-April. The trigger was direct: US President Donald Trump said a peace agreement with Iran could be signed as early as Sunday, and that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen "immediately" after the deal was inked.

A memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran, with Geneva emerging as the likeliest venue for the signing, would represent the most significant diplomatic breakthrough since the conflict began. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the deal had "never been closer," though he cautioned that the text could still change.

For India — the world's third-largest oil importer, shipping in about 90 per cent of its crude — the implications are enormous. Analysts at Aberdeen Investments have warned that India faces "a series of supply shocks" from elevated oil prices, fertiliser disruptions, and El Niño-related crop risk, all compounding at once.

## The Rupee Clawed Back Losses

The Indian rupee rallied in tandem, climbing to a one-week high of 94.96 before settling at 95.11 — up 0.7 per cent on the day. Traders unwound long dollar positions that had been built up during weeks of geopolitical stress.

"The Indian rupee clawed back Thursday's losses, buoyed by improving market sentiment as global crude prices eased and the dollar softened," said Dilip Parmar, a foreign exchange research analyst at HDFC Securities.

The Reserve Bank of India's recent measures — including a concessional forex swap facility for banks' overseas foreign-currency borrowings — have provided an additional floor. Kotak Mahindra Bank now expects the rupee to strengthen towards 93.0–93.5 in the months ahead as dollar inflows materialise.

## Banks Lead; IT Falls Further Behind

Financials led the rally, gaining over 3 per cent. Kotak Mahindra Bank, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank were among the top weekly gainers, rising roughly 6.9, 6.2, and 3.4 per cent respectively. The RBI's forex swap facility has effectively eliminated hedging costs for lenders, lowering their cost of funds and bolstering liquidity.

The midcap and smallcap indices each climbed nearly 2 per cent, signalling broad market breadth rather than a narrow large-cap rally.

The outlier was IT. The Nifty IT index fell 4.2 per cent for the week on persistent worries about AI-driven disruption to India's outsourcing sector and hot US inflation data that fuelled expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike by year-end.

## Will Foreign Money Return?

The critical question is whether the rally marks a turning point for foreign institutional flows. India has seen roughly $30 billion in foreign equity outflows since the war began — the worst stretch in decades. Analysts at Axis Direct said cooler oil prices "could reverse some of the record outflows," while two traders told Reuters that late-session buying on Friday appeared to come from foreign institutional investors rotating into financials.

For the diaspora, the rally offers a potential re-entry point. NRI investors who pulled back during the oil shock may find that a peace deal, falling crude, and a strengthening rupee create a very different risk-reward equation than the one that existed even a week ago. The Nifty snapped a two-week losing streak to end the week up 1.1 per cent. Whether that streak extends depends on what happens in Geneva on Sunday.

*Sources: Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, FXStreet, Trade Brains*
